This is the first of a two-part story looking at efforts to lower recidivism rates in California prisons.

On August 1, 1974 a young Detroit Tigers outfielder named Ron LeFlore stepped up to the plate for the first time in the major leagues. Facing the Milwaukee Brewers’ hard-throwing right-hander Jim Slaton, LeFlore didn’t do much in that at-bat or any others that day. But that inauspicious debut hardly mattered.

Almost exactly 13 months to the day prior, LeFlore had been an inmate at Michigan State Prison in Jackson, Michigan. In and out of lock-ups since he was a kid, he had served just over three years of a five-to-fifteen-year sentence for armed robbery, a crime he had committed while high on heroin.

While in prison, LeFlore discovered baseball, a sport he had never played before. A natural, he quickly became the star of the prison baseball team, good enough to draw the attention of then-Tigers manager Billy Martin. Released on July 2, 1973, LeFlore signed with the Tigers almost immediately after the gates closed behind him.

His life had officially moved from one of getting high and stealing money to chasing down high fly balls and stealing bases for a living. He would play nine years in the majors with Detroit, Montreal and the Chicago White Sox before hanging them up with more than 1,200 hits and 455 stolen bases to his credit.

LeFlore’s story is admittedly one in a million (actually the name of the 1978 made-for-TV-movie about his life starring Sacramento-native LeVar Burton), but it is exactly the kind of hopeful one that sparked legislation (AB 2204) this year from Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) that requires the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) to adopt a comprehensive statewide policy to increase opportunities for inmates to participate in organized sports.

The measure, co-authored by Assemblymembers Isaac Bryan (D-Los Angeles) and Juan Alanis (R-Modesto), further allows CDCR to enter into partnerships with colleges, universities, and professional sports teams and leagues that want to support such programs.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the bill into law on September 30th.

Gabriel told Capitol Weekly he wasn’t familiar with LeFlore when he introduced the bill, but rather had been influenced by a New York Times piece about the history of baseball in San Quentin. (He says former Assemblymember and current Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty eventually brought him up to speed on LeFlore’s story.) He was so fascinated by the piece he sent it to his staff, presuming there was already some kind of statewide policy on sports programs in state lockups.

“And they said, ‘there is none.’”

Gabriel, Bryan and Alanis went about trying to change that, and it didn’t take long for them to gain strong bipartisan support in the Legislature and from groups outside of it that rarely agree on much.

“We had a bill that’s got the police chiefs, CCPOA and all the criminal justice reform groups on the same side. And they’re all saying the same thing, which was, “We think this is a really good idea. It’s going to be good for rehabilitation. It’s going to reduce violence inside of prisons. It’s going to make communities safer when people go home.”

The measure ultimately cleared both the Assembly and Senate without a single opposing vote.

For Jacob Brevard, Chief of Programs at the Anti-Recidivism Coalition, which works to keep people from re-offending and heading back to prison, Newsom’s signature was a watershed moment in the state’s efforts to reduce recidivism.

“I think it gives people hope. It inspires them, and it makes them more confident in who they are,” he said. Brevard agrees with supporters who believe it has a good chance to also reduce violence behind prison walls.

Brevard speaks from personal experience, having served 25 years behind bars after being convicted of first-degree murder at age 19. His mother’s passing while he was inside motivated him to change his life for the better. That yearning led him to join a football team at California’s Correctional Training Facility, better known to most as Soledad State Prison.

“We had a bill that’s got the police chiefs, CCPOA and all the criminal justice reform groups on the same side. And they’re all saying the same thing, which was, “We think this is a really good idea.”

He says what he experienced in that atmosphere was life-changing.

Not that it was always easy. The game itself was nothing new – he said he had played it his whole life – but never with quite the same circumstances or the same motivation.

“I felt weird interacting with different cultures and different people that I didn’t normally associate with,” he says. “It was multicultural. There were many different members from different gangs in there. But when we was on the field, none of that mattered. It wasn’t so and so from this neighborhood, so and so from that neighborhood. It was the team name. And we all fought together on that field to make it happen.”

Brevard says being part of the team helped him learn lessons that had missed him in his younger days.

“Conflict resolution for sure,” he says. “There was a lot of huge situations that I had to learn how to work through without becoming violent. The ability to compromise, the ability to work through problems, the ability to understand that we all have roles to play.”

All of which, Gabriel said, is exactly the point.

“Sports are about a lot of things: you’re building teamwork and discipline, you’re accountable to other people, and you have to think about how your actions affect others. You have to learn how to control your emotions in heated situations. And all of these things that sports teaches are actually life lessons.”

Critical life lessons, he said, given that most incarcerated people will eventually return to society.

“How important it is to help people as they’re going through this process of rehabilitation and prepare them to go back into their communities, because the overwhelming majority of folks that are in the system are gonna come home and they’re gonna be our neighbors, right?” he said.

Like all prison reform, the path forward is not without questions. AB 2204 included what Gabriel called “seed funding” in this year’s budget, and the plan is to encourage public-private partnerships similar to how the San Francisco Giants (And the Oakland Athletics before them) offer significant financial support for the San Quentin baseball team. Future state funding would be dependent on the governor and lawmakers allocating it in the budget every year. The law is also set to expire in 2036, leaving its long-term future up to future governors and lawmakers.

Gabriel is confident his colleagues will see the program as a valuable investment both in public safety and fiscal responsibility.

“The average cost of incarceration is north of $130,000 a year per person in the system,” he said. “So anything that we can do to cut down on recidivism, anything that we can do to cut down on crime in our communities, is obviously, first and foremost, going to protect folks. But it’s also going to result in huge savings for the state.”

Sports programs are only one of the many efforts being made in California state prisons to help the incarcerated to learn life and job skills that will help them reclaim a spot in society and not return to prison. In part II of this series, we will look at the impact of other non-sports programs in reducing recidivism.
